title: p-values: What they are and how to interpret them
transcript: What we're going to talk about today is... P-Value, right? Yes, StatQuest. Hello. This is Josh Starmer. Welcome to StatQuest. Today, we will learn what a p-value is and how to interpret it. Let's assume I have two medicines. It is Medicine A... and Medicine B. And I would like to know if there is a difference between drug A and drug B. So, I gave medicine A to '1' person... and gave medicine B to another '1' person. One person who used A medicine was cured. Yay~ One person who used medicine B was not cured. Failure. Can we conclude that medicine A is better than medicine B? no! Drug B likely failed for various other reasons. This person may have taken a drug that has an adverse effect of drug B. Or you may have a rare allergic reaction to drug B. Or, this man may not have taken medication B properly, or the dosage may be incorrect. Or, drug A might not have actually worked... and a placebo effect may have occurred. When performing verification, many strange and random things can occur. This means that each drug should be tried on more than '1' person . So let's try the experiment again. This time, each medicine was given to two other people. This time, both of the two people who took medicine A were cured. Yay! And among the people who took medicine B, one was cured, and the other was not. Yay~ And failure T_T Is medicine A better? Are both medicines the same? I cannot answer two questions. This is because something strange may have happened to this person who took Medicine B. Or something strange might have happened to this person. For example, the labeling on the medicine was incorrect, so you may have actually taken Medicine A. And that might be why this person was cured. So now we are testing the drug on a very large number of people. And this is the result. Medicine A treated almost all the people. Compared to the 1,043 people who were not treated. In other words, 3 people, or 99.7% of the people who took drug A (1,046 people), were cured. Conversely, very few people have been treated with drug B. Compared to the 2 people who were not treated with drug B. 1,432 people. In other words, only 0.001% of the people who took drug B (1,434 people) were cured . If this is the result, it seems quite obvious that Drug A is better than Drug B. In other words, it is not realistic to think that 'this result was produced by arbitrary factors and there is no difference between the two drugs.' If some of these people were treated due to the placebo effect... and even if some here were not treated due to rare allergies... because there are a very large number of people treated by Drug A and a very small number treated by Drug B... it is difficult to say that this result is 'just due to something random' or that 'Drug A is not similar to Drug B.' Conversely, what if the result were like this? Only 37% of the people who took the medicine were cured. 29% of the people who took medicine B were cured. A drug treated a slightly higher percentage of people. Given that no test is perfect and there are always random factors involved... how can we be certain that Drug A is superior? This is why the p-value is needed. The P-value is a value between 0 and 1. Using the P-value, you can quantify how confident you are that there is a difference between Drug A and Drug B. If the P-value is close to 0, you can be more confident that there is a difference between drug A and drug B. Then, how small must the p-value have to be to say that there is a difference between Drug A and Drug B ? In other words, what is the threshold for making a good decision? The threshold value actually used most often is 0.05. If there is no difference between drug A and drug B, and such experiments were conducted very frequently... it means that only 5% of the experimental results are incorrect. That is correct. This is a strange sentence. So... let's look at the examples step by step. Let 's say the same drug A was given to two other groups. Now, the difference in the results is made up of 100% strange random things. These are things like rare allergies or strong placebo effects. In this case, the p-value is 0.9. It is a value much larger than 0.05. In this case, it is said that they failed to see the difference between the two groups. If the same experiment is repeated many times, in most cases, similar large p-values ​​are obtained. However, sometimes, everyone with a rare allergy can belong to the left group... and everyone with a strong placebo effect can belong to the right group. Consequently, in this specific experiment, the results are quite different, so the p-value becomes a small value of 0.01. In this case, it is said that there is a difference between the two groups even though both groups took the same medication . No! Warning: Difficult terms! Obtaining a small p-value when there is actually no difference is called a 'false positive'. A critical point for the P-value of 0.05 means that 'only the 5% experiment that differs from random factors produces a p-value less than 0.05.' In other words, if there is no difference between drug A and drug B... only 5% of the trials will have a p-value less than 0.05. This 5% experiment (wrong experiment) is called a false positive. Note: If it is very, very important to say 'there is a difference in medicine,' you may use a smaller threshold such as 0.00001. Using a threshold of 0.00001 means 'obtaining a false positive once in 100,000 experiments '. Likewise, if it is not that important... for example, in a problem like deciding whether an ice cream truck arrives on time... you can use a large threshold such as 0.2. Using a threshold of 0.2 means 'obtaining a false positive 2 out of 10 times.' Since trying to reduce false positives to less than 5% is often not cost-effective, the threshold is generally set to 0.05. In this experiment, the p-value was calculated... If the value is less than 0.05, it is determined that there is a difference between drug A and drug B. Here, the p-value is actually 0.24, so we cannot be certain that there is a difference between drug A and drug B. Bam ! great. Before wrapping up, let me mention two more things about p-values. Unfortunately, the first thing I want to talk about is a bit more of a terminological aspect. In fancy statistical terms, the attempt to determine whether or not there is a difference in medicine is called hypothesis testing. The null hypothesis is that there is no difference between the drugs. And the p-value helps us decide whether or not to accept the null hypothesis . Small baam. great. Now I know a cool term. The second thing I wanted to say is more interesting. A small p-value tells us that there is a difference between drug A and drug B, but it does not tell us how different they are. In other words, you can obtain a small p-value regardless of the magnitude of the difference between drug A and drug B. The difference can be small or large. For example, despite an 8% difference between drug A and drug B, this experiment gives a large p-value of 0.24. Conversely, in this experiment involving a very large number of people, a small p-value of 0.04 was obtained. Even in the new data given, the difference between drug A and drug B is only 1%. In summary, a small p-value does not mean that the effect size or the difference between drug A and drug B is large . Double baam!!! Yay! I finished another exciting StatQuest. If you enjoyed this StatQuest, please subscribe. Hill today's stat Quest is all about confidence intervals you may have seen or heard of confidence intervals before however if you're not not very confident about them then you're not alone many people misunderstand confidence intervals but that's only because they didn't learn about bootstrapping first now just to clarify there are lots of ways to calculate confidence intervals and bootstrapping is just one of them but for me it makes it easiest to understand but when you see confidence intervals out there in the wild you're likely to see a different way to calculate them now even though we just did bootstrapping your brain might be a little cloudy and you may have forgotten what it was all about my brain's like that so I totally understand that's why we're going to do a little bootstrap refresher imagine we weighed a bunch of female mice in this case we weighed 12 of them we didn't weigh every single female Mouse on the planet just 12 now we can take these 12 measurements and we can use them to calculate the sample mean now the sample mean is not the mean for all mice in the entire planet it's just the mean of the mice that we sampled however we can use bootstrapping and the data that we have here to determine what values would be reasonable for the global worldwide mean of all female mice on the planet now that we've calculated the sample mean we can bootstrap the sample to bootstrap the sample we randomly select 12 weights from the original sample and duplicates are okay here's an example of a bootstrapped sample we can see that this measurement on the far left was sampled twice in our bootstrap sample and the measurement to its right wasn't included in our bootstrap sample this is called sampling with replacement now we calculate the mean of the random sample after we've calculated the mean of our first random sample all we have to do is repeat steps one and two until we've calculated a lot of means sometimes more than 10,000 and here's what it looks like when we've calculated a lot of means it's maybe a little fewer than 10,000 but you get the idea anyway that's all there is to bootstrapping now let's talk about confidence intervals usually when you see a confidence interval out in the wild it's called a 95% confidence interval a 95% confidence interval is just an interval that covers 95% of the means so here we have a black bar that spans 95% of the bootstrapped means that we just calculated that's it that's all a confidence interval is nothing more nothing less can you guess what a 99% confidence interval is here's a hint it's wider than a 95% confidence interval all right I'll tell you it's just an interval that covers 99% of the means that you calculated when you bootstrapped the sample now that we know what confidence intervals are we might ask why are they useful well I think confidence intervals are useful because they are statistical tests performed visually because the interval covers 95% of the means we know that anything outside of occurs less than 5% of the time that is to say the P value of anything outside of the confidence interval is less than 05 and thus significantly different here's an example of a visual statistical test you'll remember we originally calculated the sample mean the sample mean is an estimate of the true mean for all female mice well with our confidence interval we can figure out what the the P value is that the true mean of all female mice not just of our sample is less than 20 to perform that test we draw our confidence interval which we know because of bootstrapping or some formula that we use we can see that the area left of 20 so values less than 20 are outside of our 95% confidence interval because the highlighted region is outside of the 95% confidence interval which contains 95% of the means we know that the probability that the true mean is in this area has to be less than 05 thus the P value is less than 0.05 this is unlikely and because of this we can say there's a statistically significant difference between the true mean and any value less than 20 here's another example of a visual statistical test in this case we're going to compare two samples here we've weighed female mice and now we have a sample of male mice we've already done the bootstrapping on that sample and here in the figure we just show the means from that bootstrapping because the 95% confidence intervals do not overlap we know that there is a statistically significant difference in the weights of female and male mice that is to say we know that the P value is less than 005 just by looking at the picture there is one caveat to that and to illustrate that caveat I've shifted the means a little bit over to the left so that now the confidence intervals overlap if the confidence intervals overlap there's still a chance that the means are significantly different from each other so in this case you still have to do the T Test but when the confidence intervals do not overlap then you can rest assured that there's a statistically significant difference between those two means that's all there is to it tune in next time for
